clue.text: What a prisoner does to another makes delay

parts.note: a prisoner does time, serving his sentence
another prisoner, that is, a lag, the slang word for a convict

explanation.surface: One inmate does something to a fellow inmate, and the upshot is a hold-up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'another' is short for another prisoner: an old LAG is British slang for a long-serving convict.
explanation.definitionFit: A gap of time between cause and effect is a hold-up, so the hyphenated term means a postponement.

clue.text: They will try to change rotas

parts.note: to try something is to test it

indicators.note: the letters of the next word are to be changed around

explanation.surface: Some people intend to attempt to alter the duty rosters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to change' signals an anagram of ROTAS, giving ATORS. 'They will' looks like a future tense but means people who make wills.
explanation.definitionFit: People who draw up a last testament are those who make a will.

clue.text: Swot up on one inventor

indicators.note: in a down clue up means the word is written going upward, backwards

parts.note: to swot is to cram for an exam
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Bone up on a single famous inventor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns CRAM into MARC, as in a down entry. Guglielmo Marconi pioneered radio.
explanation.definitionFit: The Italian radio pioneer was a celebrated creator of new devices.

clue.text: Asinine or owlish?

definitions.meaning: like an ass, which has big ears
like a species of owl with ear-tufts

explanation.definitionFit: Donkeys have big ears, and one owl species is named for its ear-tufts, so the term fits both creatures.

clue.text: Continue the show? Don't talk rot!

definitions.meaning: to carry on, as the show must, with a nod to a 1950s BBC radio comedy starring Spike Milligan
an exclamation of disbelief, like come off it

explanation.definitionFit: Carry on is one sense, and the exclamation of disbelief is the other; the clue also nods to a famous British radio comedy of the 1950s.

clue.text: Is such the thinking of a merrythought?

definitions.text: Is such the thinking of a merrythought?

parts.words: Is such the thinking of a merrythought?
parts.note: a merrythought is the wishbone of a fowl, so its thinking would be full of wishes

explanation.surface: A whimsical question about what a cheerful idea might be thinking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'merrythought' looks like a happy idea, but it is the old name for a bird's wishbone, and wishful thinking is the stock phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Hoping rather than reasoning is the idiom wishful thinking, which suits a bone pulled for luck when making a wish.

clue.text: Very bad quality of candle?

parts.note: evil is the moral quality, while a candle has a wick, so it is wicked in a second sense

explanation.surface: A question about how wretched a candle is.
explanation.walkthrough: A candle is 'wicked' because it has a wick; the noun for the state of being evil is read the same way.
explanation.definitionFit: Evil or sinfulness is a very bad moral quality, and a candle with a wick has it literally.

clue.text: Generate expansion? That's fine!

definitions.meaning: an exclamation of approval, like great or splendid

explanation.definitionFit: To bulge or enlarge is one sense; the other is old-fashioned slang for excellent.

clue.text: In theory they survive proper examination

parts.note: fit means suitable or proper
a test is an examination

explanation.surface: Those who pass a suitable test will, in principle, make it through.
explanation.walkthrough: The theory is Darwinian: survival of the fittest.
explanation.definitionFit: Natural selection holds that the best adapted survive, so in evolutionary theory these are the ones that endure.

clue.text: Allowed to hold Roman coin, the smallest

indicators.note: the first word is made to hold the coin inside it

parts.note: let means allowed
the as was a copper coin of ancient Rome

explanation.surface: Someone is permitted to keep an ancient coin of the lowest value.
explanation.walkthrough: The as was a small copper coin of ancient Rome, a common crossword piece; 'Allowed' must be read as a past participle, permitted.
explanation.definitionFit: Minimal or tiniest is the superlative sense of little.

clue.text: It gave suitable warning to wartime PM

definitions.text: It gave suitable warning to wartime PM

parts.words: It gave suitable warning to wartime PM
parts.note: the air-raid alarm of the Second World War was nicknamed Wailing Winnie, a fitting name given Winston Churchill was the wartime Prime Minister

explanation.surface: Something gave Churchill an appropriate alert during the war.
explanation.walkthrough: The wartime air-raid warning was nicknamed 'Wailing Winnie', the same pet name as Winston Churchill, hence 'suitable'.
explanation.definitionFit: The wailing alarm sounded before bombing raids was the device that gave the warning.

clue.text: Stalls rector has removed

indicators.note: the letters are moved about from where they stood, signalling a rearrangement

explanation.surface: A clergyman takes away some stalls, perhaps from a church fete.
explanation.walkthrough: 'removed' signals an anagram of RECTOR HAS. 'Stalls' looks like a verb or market stalls, but it means the front seats in a theatre, called the orchestra in America.
explanation.definitionFit: In American usage the ground-floor seats of a theatre are called the orchestra, the British stalls.

clue.text: In our era Gustave is much loved

indicators.note: the painter's name sits in the abbreviation for our era, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: AD, anno Domini, marks the years of our era
Gustave Doré was the French illustrator

explanation.surface: A nineteenth-century artist is much admired in modern times.
explanation.walkthrough: Gustave Doré was the French engraver famous for illustrating Dante and the Bible; 'our era' is the conventional gloss for anno Domini.
explanation.definitionFit: Being worshipped or cherished is a synonym for being greatly beloved.

clue.text: Temporary housing for Big Ben?

parts.note: Big Ben is a bell, so a portable shelter for it would be a tent for a bell

explanation.surface: A joke about putting London's famous clock bell in a makeshift shelter.
explanation.walkthrough: Big Ben is strictly the great bell in the Westminster clock tower; a bell tent is a conical camping tent.
explanation.definitionFit: A conical canvas shelter shaped like a bell is temporary accommodation, here imagined for the famous bell.

clue.text: Might be gross and still less sensitive

parts.note: even is used as still, as in even more
number means more numb, with less feeling

explanation.surface: Something could be disgusting and yet less able to feel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gross' looks like disgusting, but it is twelve dozen, 144, which divides by two. NUMBER is read as numb-er.
explanation.definitionFit: A gross is 144, divisible by two, so it is an example of such a figure.

clue.text: At each end of this plant Henry makes stockings

indicators.note: the plant with letters added at each end makes stockings, so the stockings lose those letters to leave the plant

parts.note: hosiery is the trade word for stockings and socks

indicators.note: the first and last letters of the name Henry are placed at either end

explanation.surface: A gardener named Henry somehow turns a plant into stockings.
explanation.walkthrough: Read backwards: the plant with H and Y (the first and last letters of 'Henry') at each end makes HOSIERY, so take them off HOSIERY.
explanation.definitionFit: A willow whose pliant twigs are used in basketwork is this plant.

clue.text: Change of date never treated with much respect

indicators.note: the letters of the words are changed into a new order

explanation.surface: A date was moved and never honoured properly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Change of' signals an anagram of DATE NEVER.
explanation.definitionFit: Revered or held in deep esteem is the sense of honoured with great reverence.

clue.text: Where John gave subscription for fugitive old Iranian?

parts.note: fugitive colours run, so a fugitive dye is runny
the Medes were an ancient people of Iran

explanation.surface: A question about where a ruler signed for a runaway ancient Persian.
explanation.walkthrough: King John set his seal to Magna Carta at Runnymede in 1215; 'subscription' is the old sense of signing.
explanation.definitionFit: The meadow on the Thames is where King John put his seal to Magna Carta.

clue.text: Boring characteristics of engravings

parts.note: dry means dull or boring
points are qualities or features, as in good points

explanation.surface: Engravings are said to have tedious features.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boring' could suggest drilling, which fits engraving, but it means dull.
explanation.definitionFit: Prints made by scratching a copper plate with a needle are a type of engraving.

clue.text: Plumbers' viewfinders?

parts.note: plumbers here are those who plumb the depths of water with a weighted line, measuring how deep it is

explanation.surface: A question about the sighting tools used by men who fix pipes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plumbers' suggests pipe-fitters, but to plumb is to measure depth; soundings are such measurements, also used figuratively to find out views.
explanation.definitionFit: Depth measurements taken with a lead line, or tests of opinion, are what those who plumb take.

clue.text: Strip off uniform

definitions.meaning: ordinary dress uniform, as worn off parade

explanation.definitionFit: Remove clothing is one sense; the other is the military term for everyday, informal uniform.

clue.text: Homeric bird?

parts.note: the saying goes that even Homer nods, so a bird given to nodding would be Homeric

explanation.surface: A question about a bird from the Greek epics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Even Homer nods' means even the greatest make slips; the noddy is a tropical tern.
explanation.definitionFit: The tern so named suits the proverb about the great poet dozing off.

clue.text: Doctor Silver has a broken leg to trail

parts.note: Ag is the chemical symbol for silver

indicators.note: the word leg is broken up into a new order

explanation.surface: A doctor called Silver has an injured leg and drags it behind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broken' signals an anagram of LEG, giving GLE.
explanation.definitionFit: To trail through mud or wet is to drag along the ground, which is this verb's meaning.

clue.text: Sell cheaper fillet of beef

definitions.meaning: to offer goods at a lower price than a rival
the tenderloin, a choice cut from beneath the sirloin

explanation.surface: A butcher's advice on pricing a prime cut below the competition.
explanation.definitionFit: Undersell a competitor is one sense; the other is the butcher's name for tenderloin, cut from under the ribs.

clue.text: Mouthpiece for Palatine dependency

parts.note: Palatine suggests a county palatine, but it is the palate, from which a fleshy part hangs down in the throat

explanation.surface: A spokesman for a territory ruled by a count palatine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Palatine' and 'dependency' suggest a feudal territory, but this is a piece of the mouth that depends (hangs) from the palate.
explanation.definitionFit: The fleshy lobe hanging from the soft palate is a part of the mouth.

clue.text: Irritable, rather, at typist's part being included

indicators.note: only part of the words is taken, the run included within them

explanation.surface: A rather irritated typist is involved.
explanation.walkthrough: 'part being included' points to the run RATTY inside 'rather, at typist's'.
explanation.definitionFit: Bad-tempered or tetchy is the colloquial sense, from a rat's temper.

clue.text: Translated racy number for French name-part

indicators.note: the letters are rendered into another form, as a text is put into another language

explanation.surface: Someone renders a risqué song into another language for a French singer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Translated' signals an anagram of RACY, giving CYRA.
explanation.definitionFit: Rostand's long-nosed poet is the title role of a French play, so a name-part.

clue.text: Outcry caused by the old record

parts.note: ye is an archaic form of the
an LP is a long-playing record

explanation.surface: A protest provoked by an old recording.
explanation.definitionFit: A short sharp cry of pain or alarm is a sudden shout.

clue.text: Like the quarry of Oscar's unspeakable country gentleman

definitions.text: Like the quarry of Oscar's unspeakable country gentleman

parts.words: Like the quarry of Oscar's unspeakable country gentleman
parts.note: Oscar Wilde mocked fox-hunting as the unspeakable chasing a creature nobody would want to eat; the quarry is the fox

explanation.surface: A description of what a hunting squire chases, borrowed from Wilde.
explanation.walkthrough: Wilde's line on fox-hunting: 'the unspeakable in full pursuit of the uneatable'. The quarry is the fox, the unspeakable the English country gentleman.
explanation.definitionFit: A fox is not fit to be consumed, so Wilde's quarry is described as unfit for the table.

clue.text: Early introducer of ball-game from Greece?

definitions.text: Early introducer of ball-game from Greece?

parts.words: Early introducer of ball-game from Greece?
parts.note: the lord who brought the Parthenon sculptures to London is pictured as importing a game of marbles

explanation.surface: A question about who first brought a sport to Britain from Greece.
explanation.walkthrough: Lord Elgin removed the Parthenon sculptures, the Elgin Marbles, to Britain; marbles is also a children's game played with small glass balls.
explanation.definitionFit: The earl who shipped the Parthenon marbles to Britain is jokingly the importer of the game of marbles.

clue.text: In role of speaker he proves mettle, I hear

parts.note: as means in the capacity of
a sayer is one who says things

explanation.surface: An actor taking the role of an orator shows his courage, so I'm told.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is itself a sound-alike: an assayer tests metal, which sounds like 'mettle', hence 'I hear'.
explanation.definitionFit: A tester of ores checks the purity of metal, which spoken sounds the same as courage.

clue.text: She's entitled to look closely at oriental vessel

parts.note: to peer is to look closely
E for East, as in oriental
SS is a steamship

explanation.surface: A woman has every right to examine an eastern vase carefully.
explanation.walkthrough: 'entitled' means having a title, not having a right.
explanation.definitionFit: A noblewoman holding a rank in her own right or by marriage bears a title.
